what_they_do: Resourcly reads technical drawings, datasheets, and other parts records scattered across a manufacturer's PLM and ERP systems and automatically figures out which parts are actually duplicates or interchangeable, even when different plants or suppliers name and code them differently. It then recommends and helps execute the fix: reusing an existing part instead of ordering a new one, standardizing variants, consolidating suppliers, or pooling excess inventory across divisions. This replaces the manual process where engineers and procurement teams cross-reference specs by hand across fragmented systems to find redundant parts and free up working capital tied up in idle inventory.
vertical: Industrial manufacturing (parts master data harmonization / inventory optimization)
theme_fit_rationale: Resourcly's core wedge is ingesting unstructured documents (technical drawings, datasheets) that legacy PLM/ERP systems can't read, then using that as the entry point to automate downstream procurement and inventory workflows, the exact pattern in Theme 5. The drawing-reading capability is also a vision-based model applied to a manufacturing workflow, fitting Theme 1 as a secondary lens.
workflow_artifacts: sustainability data (carbon footprint, recyclability, critical substances)
prior_insights: Was talking to a procurement lead at a mid-sized manufacturer recently and they estimated 15-20% of their parts catalog is redundant. Curious how you're approaching the data normalization piece.

I was reading the CPO Strategy piece about Resourcly and the Sandvik example stood out. The idea that manufacturers are sitting on billions in idle parts not because the parts are broken, but because they're buried across fragmented PLM and ERP systems, is something I keep hearing from procurement teams. I think the similarity analysis approach, where you're actually comparing technical drawings and datasheets to find interchangeable parts, is what separates this from just another data cleanup project. Most spend analytics tools can tell you that you're buying too many variants, but they can't tell you which ones are actually interchangeable. Curious whether the sustainability angle, tracking carbon footprints and recyclability at the part level, is something customers are asking for or if it's more of a differentiator you're leading with proactively.

Saw you guys just closed a seed round last month, congrats. I was looking at the redundant parts detection angle and I think the consolidation story resonates most with procurement teams at mid-market manufacturers who are sitting on bloated supplier lists they inherited from acquisitions or organic growth. Chris has worked with Paperless Parts and Project44 on the manufacturing and supply chain side. Curious how the German market compares to what you're seeing in the US in terms of appetite for this.
